title: Environments and CI/CD
summary: Why Notely runs in three places (local, preview, production), how each gets its own settings and data, and how automatic checks stop broken code before it deploys.
youWillLearn: The three environments and what each one is for
How environment variables let the same code talk to different databases
What CI runs on every pull request, and how a red check blocks a merge
Why production secrets must never reach preview builds

glossary.environment: One place your app runs, with its own settings and data: your laptop, a preview URL, or the live site.
glossary.environment variable: A named setting given to the app from outside the code, like a database URL or an API key.
glossary.preview deployment: A temporary copy of the app built from one branch, with its own URL, for checking before merging.
glossary.staging: A shared test environment set up like production but filled with fake data.
glossary.CI: Continuous integration: a robot that runs your checks (lint, types, tests) on every push.
glossary.CD: Continuous deployment: every merge to main is built and released automatically.
glossary.pipeline: The fixed sequence of steps code goes through from push to live: install, check, build, deploy.
glossary.required check: A CI job that must pass before GitHub lets anyone merge a pull request.
glossary.lint: An automatic read-through of the code that flags likely mistakes and style problems.

steps.title: One database for everything
body: Maya is testing a new delete-all-notes feature on her laptop. Her .env.local holds the same database URL as the live app.
She clicks the button to try it. Real users' notes disappear. Nothing was wrong with her laptop. It was talking to the one database that mattered.

callout.text: Rehearsing a play on the real stage, during the real show, in front of the paying audience.

scene.caption: Laptop, preview and live app all share the production database.

steps.title: Three places, three sets of data
body: The fix is to run the same code in separate environments, each with its own data.

Local: your laptop, with a local or throwaway database. Preview: a URL per branch, using test data. Production: the real app and the only place with real users. A mistake in the first two costs nothing.

scene.caption: Each environment has its own database. Only production touches real data.

steps.title: Same code, different settings
body: How does one codebase know which database to use? Environment variables. The code reads process.env.SUPABASE_URL, and each environment fills in a different value.
On your laptop they live in .env.local, which is never committed. On Vercel you set them per environment: Development, Preview and Production.

code.caption: vercel env pull .env.local copies the Development values from Vercel to your laptop.

callout.text: In Next.js, any variable starting with NEXT_PUBLIC_ is copied into the browser bundle, where anyone can read it. Only public values go there. Never the Claude API key or the Supabase service role key.

scene.caption: The same code reads a different database URL in each environment.

steps.title: A preview for every branch
body: Each pull request gets a preview deployment: a real build of that branch at its own URL. Send it to a client, test on your phone, click every state.
Previews should point at test data. That can be one shared staging database, or a fresh database branch per PR if your Supabase plan offers branching.

callout.text: For client work, the preview link is your review tool. Sam approves the booking flow on the preview, then you merge. No "it looked different on my screen" surprises.

scene.caption: Maya's branch gets its own URL, wired to the test database.

steps.title: CI: a robot checks every push
body: Separate environments protect data. CI protects code. On every push, a machine installs the app and runs the same checks every time: lint, type check, tests, build.
Then CD takes over: merge to main and production deploys on its own. The whole route, push to live, is the pipeline.

callout.text: A preflight checklist. The pilot is experienced, and still runs the same list before every take-off, because forgetting one item once is enough.

scene.caption: Push, check, build, deploy. Every change takes the same route.

steps.title: The CI file, line by line
body: On GitHub, CI is a YAML file in .github/workflows/. This one runs on every pull request and every push to main.
Each run line is a command you could type yourself. If any command fails, the job turns red and the rest stop. Vercel builds and deploys separately, through its GitHub integration.

code.code:
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with: { node-version: lts/*, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npx tsc --noEmit
      - run: npm test
code.caption: npm ci installs exactly what the lockfile says, so CI matches your laptop.

callout.text: Ask Claude Code to add this file, then check: does every script it calls exist in package.json? Does it run on pull_request? Are secrets read from ${{ secrets.NAME }}, never pasted in? Push a deliberately broken commit once to see it turn red.

scene.caption: Every check in the file runs in order. All green: the preview goes up.

steps.title: Red check, locked door
body: A check that only warns gets ignored on busy days. Make it a required check: in the repo settings, add a branch protection rule (or ruleset) on main that requires the CI job to pass.
Now a pull request with a failing test cannot be merged, by you, a teammate, or Claude Code. Broken code stops before production, not after.

scene.caption: One test fails. The merge button is locked, so production never sees the bug.

steps.title: Production secrets stay in production
body: A tempting shortcut: copy every production variable into Preview "so it works". Now every preview URL, the ones you send to clients and testers, reads and writes real data with full-power keys.
Give Preview its own test database and its own API keys with low limits. If a preview leaks, nothing real is exposed.

callout.text: Vercel's Preview variables apply to every branch. A half-finished branch with a bug and a production service role key is a data breach waiting for a link to be shared.

scene.caption: A preview holding production keys reaches straight into real data.

steps.title: Recap: separate places, automatic gates
body: Run the same code in three environments: local, preview, production. Environment variables point each one at its own data and keys, and only production touches real users.
CI runs the same checks on every push. Make them required, and a red check blocks the merge. Merging to main is then the only way to deploy.

quiz.question: Maya wants to try a migration that drops a column. Where should she run it first?

options.text: On production, late at night when traffic is low.
options.why: Low traffic does not make a dropped column come back. Try destructive changes where data is fake.

options.text: Locally or on a preview database, then production after it works.
options.why: That is what non-production environments are for. A mistake there costs a reset, not real users' data.
Backups help you recover, but restoring is slow and loses recent changes. Prevention is far cheaper.

quiz.question: Claude Code added NEXT_PUBLIC_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY so the browser can call Claude directly. What is wrong?

options.text: Nothing, as long as the variable is set on Vercel and not committed.
options.why: Where it is stored does not matter. The NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix copies the value into the JavaScript every visitor downloads.

options.text: The name is too long for Vercel.
options.why: The name is fine. The prefix is the problem.

options.text: The key is shipped to every browser. Call Claude from a server route with a private variable.
options.why: Anyone can open the bundle and spend your credits. The key must stay on the server, behind your own API route.

quiz.question: Your CI runs tests on every pull request, but last week someone merged a PR with a failing test anyway. What fixes this?

options.text: Make the CI job a required check on main.
options.why: A required check turns the result into a gate. GitHub will not allow a merge until the job passes.

options.text: Run the tests again after the merge.
options.why: That finds the bug after it is already on its way to production.

options.text: Ask everyone to look at the checks before merging.
options.why: Good intentions fail on busy days. A rule the machine enforces does not.

takeaways: Run the same code in three environments: local, preview, production. Only production touches real data.
Environment variables carry the differences. NEXT_PUBLIC_ values are public; secrets never get that prefix.
Every pull request gets a preview URL. Point it at test data, never at production keys.
CI runs lint, types and tests on every push. Make it a required check so red blocks the merge.
